title: Backend entry domain api pagination versioning
topic: Backend entry domain api pagination versioning
question: Why does a list endpoint like GET /posts need pagination, and what are the tradeoffs between offset-based and cursor-based pagination?
idealAnswer:
Without pagination, a growing table means the endpoint eventually returns huge, slow responses and risks timing out or exhausting memory on both server and client

Offset-based pagination (LIMIT/OFFSET) is simple and supports jumping to an arbitrary page, but gets slower as the offset grows (the database still has to scan/skip past all prior rows) and can skip or duplicate items if rows are inserted/deleted between page requests

Cursor-based pagination uses a pointer (often the last seen id or timestamp) to fetch the next page, staying fast regardless of how deep you page, and is stable under concurrent inserts/deletes, but doesn't support jumping to an arbitrary page number

Mentions API versioning at a basic level, e.g. why you'd version an API (URL path like /v1/, or a header) so existing clients don't break when the response shape changes

Bonus: connects pagination choice to the use case, e.g. an admin dashboard with page numbers might prefer offset for UX, an infinite-scroll feed prefers cursor for correctness and performance

title: Backend entry domain authn sessions tokens
topic: Backend entry domain authn sessions tokens
question: Compare session-based authentication with token-based authentication (like JWTs). How does each keep track of who's logged in?
idealAnswer:
Session-based: server creates a session record (often in memory or a store like Redis) after login, gives the client an opaque session ID in a cookie, and looks up the session on every request

Token-based: server issues a signed token (e.g. JWT) containing claims about the user, the client sends it on every request, and the server verifies the signature without needing to look anything up

Explains the key tradeoff: sessions are easy to revoke instantly (just delete the server-side record) but require server-side state and a shared store across instances, tokens are stateless and scale easily but are hard to revoke before they expire

Mentions where each token typically lives on the client (cookie vs local storage/header) and at least a passing awareness of the security implications, e.g. cookies with httpOnly help against XSS reading them, but need CSRF protection

Doesn't confuse authentication (who are you) with authorization (what are you allowed to do), even though both mechanisms are usually used to support both

title: Backend entry domain sql joins indexes
topic: Backend entry domain sql joins indexes
question: Explain the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN, and explain what a database index actually does to speed up a query.
idealAnswer:
INNER JOIN returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables, LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matched rows from the right, with NULLs filling in where there's no match

Gives a concrete scenario where the difference matters, e.g. listing all users including ones with zero orders requires LEFT JOIN, INNER JOIN would silently drop them

Explains an index as a separate, ordered data structure (commonly a B-tree) that lets the database find matching rows without scanning the whole table

Connects indexes to the columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses, an index only helps if the query can actually use it

Mentions the tradeoff: indexes speed up reads but add overhead to writes (every insert/update/delete has to update the index too) and take up storage

topic: Backend entry scenario counter race condition
question: You built a 'view count' feature: each page view runs 'read the current count, add 1, save it back'. Under heavy traffic, the count ends up lower than the actual number of views. Why, and how would you fix it?
idealAnswer:
Identifies the lost update problem: two requests can both read the same starting count before either writes back, so one increment gets silently overwritten by the other

Explains this gets worse under concurrency/load precisely because more requests overlap in that read-modify-write window

Proposes an atomic update as the fix, e.g. UPDATE counts SET count = count + 1 WHERE id = ..., which lets the database do the increment in one step instead of round-tripping through the application

Recognizes this is a general pattern (read-modify-write without atomicity), not a one-off bug, and that the fix is to push the operation into the database rather than trying to synchronize application code

Bonus: mentions alternatives like a database-level increment counter, or an atomic increment in something like Redis if the counter doesn't need to live in the primary database

title: Backend entry scenario n plus one
topic: Backend entry scenario n plus one
question: An endpoint that lists 20 blog posts along with each post's author name is making 21 separate database queries per request. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
idealAnswer:
Identifies this as the classic N+1 query problem: one query for the list, then N more queries (one per row) for related data

Explains why it's slow: each extra query has its own round-trip latency, so the cost scales linearly with the number of rows instead of staying constant

Proposes fixing it with a JOIN to fetch posts and authors in a single query, or a batched second query (e.g. fetch all needed author ids at once with WHERE id IN (...)) instead of one query per row

Recognizes that this pattern often hides inside ORMs via lazy-loading relations, and that awareness of what the ORM is actually generating (e.g. via query logging) is important to catch it

Bonus: notes the tradeoff between a single wide JOIN (simpler, but can duplicate data if there are multiple joined rows) versus a batched second query (slightly more code, avoids duplication)

title: Backend entry scenario slow endpoint
topic: Backend entry scenario slow endpoint
question: GET /users/:id/orders used to respond in under 100ms and now takes 3 seconds. How would you go about figuring out why?
idealAnswer:
Starts by reproducing and measuring rather than guessing, e.g. checking logs/APM for where the time is actually going (database query vs application code vs network)

Suspects the database query first given the growth in table size, and would check whether there's an index on the foreign key used in the query (e.g. orders.user_id)

Would look at the query plan (e.g. EXPLAIN) to see if it's doing a full table scan instead of an index lookup

Considers that the endpoint might be returning way more rows than needed (no pagination or limit), making both the query and the JSON serialization slower as data grows

Mentions verifying the fix with a measurement afterward, not just assuming the change worked

title: Backend mid domain caching strategies
topic: Backend mid domain caching strategies
question: Compare cache-aside and write-through caching strategies. When would you reach for each?
idealAnswer:
Cache-aside (lazy loading): application checks the cache first, on a miss reads from the database and populates the cache, writes go directly to the database and either invalidate or update the cache entry

Write-through: every write goes through the cache, which writes to the database synchronously, so the cache is always up to date and reads are guaranteed fresh, at the cost of every write paying cache-write latency

Explains staleness tradeoffs: cache-aside can serve stale data if invalidation is missed or delayed, write-through avoids that but adds write latency and complexity

Mentions cache invalidation as the hard part in practice, e.g. TTLs as a simple safety net, and the difficulty of invalidating exactly the right keys when underlying data changes

Gives a sensible use case for each: cache-aside for read-heavy data that's expensive to compute and tolerates brief staleness (e.g. product listings), write-through for data where reads must reflect the latest write immediately after it happens

title: Backend mid domain message queues async
topic: Backend mid domain message queues async
question: Why would you put a message queue between two services instead of having one call the other directly, and what do you give up by doing that?
idealAnswer:
Decouples the producer and consumer in time: the producer can keep going even if the consumer is slow or temporarily down, since the message just waits in the queue

Smooths out load spikes, the consumer processes at its own sustainable rate instead of being overwhelmed by a burst of direct calls (buffering/backpressure)

Enables retries and durability: a failed processing attempt can be retried, or sent to a dead-letter queue for inspection, without the original caller needing to know or care

Names the cost: it trades a simple synchronous request/response (caller knows immediately if it worked) for eventual, asynchronous processing, plus the operational overhead of running and monitoring the queue itself

Mentions at-least-once delivery as the common default guarantee, and that consumers therefore need to handle receiving the same message more than once (idempotent processing)

title: Backend mid domain rate limiting approaches
topic: Backend mid domain rate limiting approaches
question: Compare token bucket, fixed window, and sliding window as rate limiting algorithms, and explain the failure mode of the naive one.
idealAnswer:
Fixed window: counts requests in a fixed time bucket (e.g. per minute) and resets at the boundary, simple to implement but allows a burst of up to 2x the limit right around the boundary (e.g. a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again immediately at the start of the next)

Sliding window (log or counter-based approximation): tracks requests over a continuously moving window rather than a hard reset, avoiding the boundary burst problem at the cost of more bookkeeping

Token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate up to a max capacity, each request consumes a token, naturally allows brief bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a steady average rate over time

Explains why token bucket is often preferred in practice, it allows legitimate bursty traffic (a user clicking rapidly) while still bounding sustained rate, which fixed window can't do gracefully

Mentions that in a distributed system, whichever algorithm is chosen needs a shared store (like Redis) with atomic increment/check operations, or the limit isn't actually enforced correctly across multiple server instances

title: Backend mid domain transactions isolation levels
topic: Backend mid domain transactions isolation levels
question: What does a database transaction guarantee, and what's the practical difference between Read Committed and Serializable isolation levels?
idealAnswer:
Explains ACID at least at a working level, and specifically what a transaction guarantees: a set of operations either all happen or none do (atomicity), and the database moves from one valid state to another (consistency), with some degree of isolation from concurrent transactions, and durability once committed

Read Committed: a transaction only ever sees data that's been committed by other transactions, but if it reads the same row twice, it can see different values if another transaction committed a change in between (non-repeatable read)

Serializable: the strongest level, transactions behave as if they ran one at a time in some order, eliminating non-repeatable reads and phantom reads, but at the cost of more locking/blocking or more transaction retries on conflict

Gives a concrete example of a bug that Read Committed allows but Serializable prevents, e.g. two transactions both reading an account balance, both deciding it's sufficient for a withdrawal, and both proceeding

Connects isolation level choice to a real tradeoff: stricter isolation reduces anomalies but reduces throughput/concurrency, so the right level depends on how much correctness risk the specific operation can tolerate

title: Backend mid scenario connection pool exhaustion
topic: Backend mid scenario connection pool exhaustion
question: Under moderate traffic, your API starts throwing 'timeout waiting for connection from pool' errors, even though the database itself isn't overloaded. What's happening, and how do you fix it?
idealAnswer:
Identifies that all connections in the pool are tied up, likely held by the slow report query (or several concurrent instances of it) for longer than usual, starving every other request of a connection

Would check for connections not being released properly too, e.g. a code path that opens a connection and doesn't close/return it on an error path, slowly leaking pool capacity over time

Proposes fixes: adding a query timeout so a slow query can't hold a connection indefinitely, and/or moving the slow report query to a separate pool or a read replica so it can't starve the main request path

Considers pool sizing itself, but recognizes that just increasing pool size is a band-aid if the real problem is one query hogging connections for too long, and can push too many connections onto the database itself

Mentions adding monitoring/alerting on pool utilization so this is caught before it causes user-facing timeouts next time

question: Your database logs show periodic deadlock errors between two transactions, and some requests are failing as a result. How do you investigate and fix it?
idealAnswer:
Identifies the root cause pattern: two transactions acquiring the same two locks in opposite orders is the classic recipe for a deadlock, the database detects the cycle and kills one transaction to break it

Would pull the actual deadlock log/trace to confirm which tables and rows were involved rather than guessing

Proposes the standard fix: enforce a consistent lock acquisition order across all code paths (e.g. always touch accounts before transfers, everywhere), which eliminates the possibility of a cycle

Mentions handling the immediate symptom too, the losing transaction should be retried by the application (deadlocks are expected to happen occasionally even with good ordering, under real concurrency), not just left to fail

Considers keeping transactions short and touching as few rows as possible to reduce the window where a deadlock can occur, in addition to fixing the ordering

title: Backend mid scenario idempotent payment retry
topic: Backend mid scenario idempotent payment retry
question: A client calls POST /charge to charge a customer's card, the request times out on the client side, and the client automatically retries. How do you make sure the customer isn't charged twice?
idealAnswer:
Recognizes that a client-side timeout doesn't tell you whether the server-side operation actually completed, so simply 'not getting a response' can't be trusted to mean 'nothing happened'

Proposes an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical charge attempt (not per HTTP request) and sends it with every retry, the server stores which keys it has already processed and returns the original result instead of charging again

Explains the storage needs to be checked and written atomically (e.g. a unique constraint on the idempotency key in the database) so two near-simultaneous retries can't both slip through the check

Considers what to return while the original request is still in flight (not yet finished) when a retry with the same key arrives, so the retry doesn't race ahead of the original

Mentions that many payment processors support idempotency keys natively, and a strong answer would pass the same key through to the processor as well, not just dedupe at the API layer

title: Backend mid scenario zero downtime migration
topic: Backend mid scenario zero downtime migration
question: You need to rename a column that's actively read and written by a live service handling continuous traffic, with no maintenance window. How do you do it safely?
idealAnswer:
Rejects the naive single-step rename, since a rolling deploy means old and new application code run simultaneously against the same database for a period, and either version would break if the column were renamed atomically

Proposes an expand-and-contract (multi-step) approach: first add the new column alongside the old one, deploy code that writes to both, backfill existing rows, then deploy code that reads from the new column, and only drop the old column once nothing references it

Explains why each step needs to be independently safe and backward-compatible, so the deploy can proceed instance by instance without any window where some instances break

Considers backfilling large tables carefully, e.g. in batches, to avoid a single long-running migration that locks the table or overloads the database

Mentions verifying (e.g. via logging or a temporary check) that nothing is still reading the old column before actually dropping it, rather than assuming the code changes were complete

Proposes a queue-based architecture: internal services enqueue a notification request and return immediately, a set of workers consume the queue and actually call the relevant provider (email/SMS/push), decoupling callers from provider latency and failures

Designs a reasonably provider-agnostic internal API/schema (recipient, channel, template, payload) so callers don't need to know provider-specific details, and providers can be swapped without changing callers

Handles provider failures with retries and backoff, and a dead-letter queue or failure table for notifications that repeatedly fail, rather than silently dropping them

Addresses idempotency/deduplication, e.g. a retry of the same enqueue request (or a caller's own retry) shouldn't result in the user getting the same notification twice

Considers user preferences and rate limits, e.g. not spamming a user with the same type of notification repeatedly, and respecting opt-outs, as a first-class part of the design rather than an afterthought

title: Backend senior domain database sharding
topic: Backend senior domain database sharding
question: When a single database can no longer handle the write load, what are the main sharding strategies, and what do you give up with each?
idealAnswer:
Explains sharding as splitting data across multiple database instances by some key, so no single instance holds or serves all the data or write traffic

Hash-based sharding: a hash of the shard key determines the shard, giving an even distribution and avoiding hot spots, but makes range queries (e.g. 'all orders from last week') expensive since matching rows are scattered across every shard

Range-based sharding: contiguous key ranges live on the same shard, making range queries efficient, but risks hot spots if writes cluster in one range (e.g. sharding by signup date puts all of today's traffic on one shard)

Discusses the operational cost that cuts across both: cross-shard joins and transactions become hard or impossible, so schema and query design have to actively avoid needing them, and resharding (changing shard count) later is a genuinely difficult migration

Mentions picking a shard key deliberately based on access patterns (e.g. shard by tenant/customer id if most queries are scoped to one customer), not just an arbitrary column, since the wrong key forces cross-shard queries constantly

title: Backend senior domain distributed consensus
topic: Backend senior domain distributed consensus
question: Why is getting a group of machines to agree on a single value (distributed consensus) considered hard, and what problem does something like Raft actually solve?
idealAnswer:
Frames the core difficulty correctly: in an asynchronous network you can't reliably distinguish a slow node from a crashed one, so any protocol has to make progress despite genuine ambiguity about node state

Explains that naive approaches (e.g. just trust whichever node responds first, or a fixed primary with no failover) break down when nodes crash, messages are delayed or lost, or the network partitions, because you can end up with two nodes both believing they're in charge (split brain)

Describes what a consensus protocol like Raft provides at a conceptual level: leader election so exactly one node coordinates writes at a time, and a way to replicate a log of operations so a majority of nodes agree on the order of operations even if some nodes are down

Connects majority/quorum-based agreement to fault tolerance, a cluster of 2f+1 nodes can keep making progress despite f failures, because any two majorities always overlap in at least one node

Gives a concrete example of where this matters in practice, e.g. electing a primary database node, or coordinating configuration in systems like etcd/ZooKeeper that other services rely on for correctness

title: Backend senior domain exactly once delivery
topic: Backend senior domain exactly once delivery
question: People often say 'exactly-once delivery is impossible' in distributed systems, but plenty of production systems claim to offer it. How do you reconcile that?
idealAnswer:
Explains why true exactly-once at the network/transport level is impossible: you can't distinguish a lost acknowledgment from a lost message, so a sender genuinely cannot know whether to retry without risking a duplicate

Distinguishes delivery semantics clearly: at-most-once (send and forget, can lose messages), at-least-once (retry until acknowledged, can duplicate), and explains that what's usually called 'exactly-once' is really at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing on the receiving end

Describes how systems actually achieve effectively-once processing: deduplication using a unique message id or idempotency key, so a duplicate delivery is detected and discarded (or produces the same result) rather than being reprocessed

Mentions that this dedup step itself has to be atomic with the side effect it's guarding (e.g. writing 'processed message X' and applying its effect in the same transaction), otherwise a crash between the two steps reopens the same gap

Gives a concrete example, e.g. Kafka's idempotent producer plus transactional consumer offsets, or a payment processor using idempotency keys, as effectively-once in practice built on top of at-least-once delivery

title: Backend senior scenario build vs buy
topic: Backend senior scenario build vs buy
question: Your team needs full-text search over product data, and the launch deadline is six weeks out. Do you build a custom search index or adopt a managed search service like Elasticsearch/Algolia? How do you actually decide, under time pressure, rather than just picking whichever you're more comfortable with?
idealAnswer:
Frames the decision around the team's actual constraints, not a generic pros/cons list: six weeks strongly favors adopting something proven, since building and hardening a custom index (relevance tuning, scaling, operational maturity) rarely fits that timeline well even for an experienced team

Weighs the real cost of 'buy', not just licensing, but the ongoing operational burden of a new piece of infrastructure the team has never run, and evaluates whether that's a reasonable ask alongside everything else in flight

Considers whether the requirement is actually as core and differentiated as it seems, if search relevance itself isn't a competitive differentiator for this product, that argues further toward not spending scarce engineering time building it from scratch

Identifies what would change the calculus, e.g. if the deadline were 6 months rather than 6 weeks, or if search quality were the core product value proposition, note explicitly that the decision isn't universal, it's conditional on the actual constraints

Talks about avoiding lock-in risk with a buy decision by keeping a clean data-access boundary (so the search backend could be swapped later) rather than treating the choice as permanent and irreversible

title: Backend senior scenario cascading outage
topic: Backend senior scenario cascading outage
question: A downstream service starts responding slowly. Within a few minutes, every service that calls it is also degraded, and the whole platform is effectively down. As the engineer leading incident response, what do you do?
idealAnswer:
Leads with stabilizing the system before root-causing it, e.g. shedding load or failing fast on calls to the slow downstream service (even manually, like scaling it down from the load balancer or feature-flagging off the dependent functionality) to stop the cascade from spreading further

Correctly diagnoses the mechanism: callers are blocking and holding resources (threads, connections) waiting on a slow dependency, so the slowness of one service propagates as resource exhaustion in every caller, not just as slow responses

Talks about clear incident command basics: someone owning the decision-making and communication, status updates going out, avoiding multiple people making uncoordinated changes to the same systems mid-incident

Identifies the durable fix for next time: timeouts and circuit breakers on inter-service calls, so one slow dependency degrades gracefully (fails fast, or serves cached/default data) instead of cascading

Mentions a blameless postmortem afterward focused on why the cascade wasn't contained (missing timeouts/circuit breakers, no load shedding), not just what triggered the initial slowness

title: Backend senior scenario schema migration disagreement
topic: Backend senior scenario schema migration disagreement
question: A teammate wants to add a new required field to a heavily used shared table by writing directly to production during a deploy, arguing it's simple and other approaches are overkill. You think it needs the full expand-and-contract migration process. How do you handle the disagreement?
idealAnswer:
Engages with the actual technical risk concretely rather than just asserting process for its own sake, e.g. explains specifically what breaks: services running old code during a rolling deploy will fail on the new required field, or existing rows without a value will violate the constraint

Acknowledges that the migration process has a real cost (more steps, more time) and doesn't pretend that's free, the disagreement is a genuine tradeoff between speed and risk, not a simple right-versus-wrong situation

Tries to find out why past 'quick' changes didn't cause incidents, e.g. lower traffic at the time, no concurrent readers, smaller blast radius, rather than treating past luck as proof the approach is safe in general

Since other teams depend on the table, brings them into the decision rather than resolving it unilaterally between the two people making the change, since they're the ones who'd be affected by an outage

Has a clear fallback if agreement can't be reached, e.g. escalating to a lead/staff engineer for a decision, or proposing a middle ground like doing it safely but on an accelerated timeline, rather than either steamrolling the teammate or silently letting a risky change ship

Recognizes the core tension: exact global counting requires cross-region coordination on every request, which conflicts directly with the latency requirement, so the design has to trade off strict accuracy for speed

Proposes a workable approach, e.g. splitting the global budget into per-region sub-limits (with periodic rebalancing based on observed traffic share), or an asynchronous replication of counts between regions with a tolerance for some overshoot

Explains why naive synchronous cross-region locking/counting on every request is a non-starter given the stated latency constraints, and articulates that explicitly as a rejected approach rather than skipping it

Addresses staleness explicitly: whichever approach is chosen, defines the bound on how far off the enforced limit can be from the true global count, and argues why that's an acceptable tradeoff for this use case

topic: Backend senior systemdesign payments system
question: Design the core backend for processing payments: a customer pays for an order, the money needs to move correctly, and the books need to stay accurate even when things fail partway through.

Treats correctness of money movement as the central constraint and designs around it, e.g. an append-only ledger of transactions rather than only mutable balance fields, so the full history of how a balance was reached is always reconstructable and auditable

Handles the processor's uncertain outcomes (timeout, unclear success/failure) with idempotency keys on every charge attempt, and a reconciliation step that queries the processor's actual state for any payment left in an ambiguous status, rather than assuming failure and retrying blindly

Models a payment as a state machine (e.g. created, pending, succeeded, failed, refunded) with explicit, valid transitions, so partial failures land in a well-defined state instead of an ambiguous one

Addresses idempotency at the API layer as well, so a client's retried request for the same logical payment doesn't create a duplicate charge, distinct from idempotency between this service and the processor

Considers eventual consistency between 'payment succeeded' and dependent state (like marking an order as paid), e.g. via an event the order service consumes, and explains why doing both in one atomic step usually isn't possible when the processor is an external system

question: When would you prefer the median over the mean to summarize a dataset, and what does standard deviation tell you that the mean alone doesn't?
idealAnswer:
The mean is sensitive to outliers, a few extreme values can pull it far from where most of the data actually sits

The median, the middle value when sorted, is robust to outliers and better represents a typical value in skewed distributions, e.g. income or house prices

The mean alone says nothing about spread, two datasets can have the same mean but very different variability

Standard deviation measures how spread out values are around the mean, a small standard deviation means values cluster tightly, a large one means they're spread widely

title: Data entry domain data types schemas
topic: Data entry domain data types schemas
question: What is a schema, and what's the difference between schema-on-write and schema-on-read?
idealAnswer:
A schema defines the structure of data: field names, data types, and constraints like nullability or uniqueness

Schema-on-write enforces the structure before data is stored, e.g. a traditional relational database rejects a row that doesn't match the table definition

Schema-on-read stores data in a more flexible or raw form, e.g. files in a data lake, and the structure is applied only when the data is queried or read

Schema-on-write catches data quality problems early but is less flexible if the source data changes shape often

Schema-on-read is more flexible and lets you store diverse data cheaply, but pushes the risk of malformed or unexpected data downstream to whoever reads it

title: Data entry domain etl vs elt
topic: Data entry domain etl vs elt
question: What is the difference between ETL and ELT, and why might a team choose one over the other?
idealAnswer:
ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) transforms data before it lands in the destination system, so the warehouse only ever holds clean, modeled data

ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into the destination first, and transformation happens afterward using the destination's own compute, e.g. a cloud warehouse

ELT became more common as cloud warehouses got cheap, elastic compute, since transformations can be pushed down and rerun without re-extracting from source systems

ETL can be preferable when the destination has limited compute, when sensitive data must be filtered or masked before it lands anywhere, or for compliance reasons

ELT keeps raw data around, which makes it easier to reprocess or debug when transformation logic changes, since you are not stuck with only the already-transformed version

question: What is a DataFrame, and how do you handle missing values in one?
idealAnswer:
A DataFrame is a two-dimensional, labeled table structure, e.g. in pandas, with rows and typed columns, similar in spirit to a database table or spreadsheet

Missing values commonly show up as NaN or null, and can arise from failed joins, optional fields, or upstream data issues

Common strategies include dropping rows or columns with missing values, when the amount missing is small and dropping won't bias the analysis

Imputation fills missing values with something reasonable, e.g. mean, median, a constant, or a value derived from other columns, but the choice of imputation method can itself bias results

A strong answer notes that blindly filling or dropping without first checking why data is missing, e.g. missing not at random, can introduce bias into downstream analysis

title: Data entry domain sql joins window functions
topic: Data entry domain sql joins window functions
question: Explain the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN, and describe a case where you'd reach for a window function instead of a GROUP BY.
idealAnswer:
INNER JOIN only returns rows where the join key matches in both tables, rows without a match on either side are dropped

LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, filling in NULLs for columns from the right table when there is no match, which is useful when you don't want to silently lose rows

GROUP BY collapses rows into one row per group, so you lose the individual row-level detail

A window function, e.g. ROW_NUMBER, RANK, SUM OVER PARTITION BY, computes an aggregate per row while still returning one row per original record, useful for things like running totals or ranking within a group

A concrete example: ranking each customer's orders by date to find their most recent order, without collapsing the other order rows away

title: Data entry scenario sampling bias survey

question: What's the problem with concluding this from the survey, and how would you fix how the data was collected?
idealAnswer:
The sample is drawn only from customers who contacted support, which is not representative of the full customer base, most satisfied customers never contact support at all

This is a form of sampling bias, specifically a selection bias, the conclusion about overall satisfaction doesn't generalize beyond the surveyed group

Response bias is also a concern, people who respond to surveys often have stronger opinions, positive or negative, than the average customer, skewing the average

A better approach would sample from the entire customer population, not just those who self-selected into contacting support

A strong answer suggests randomly sampling across all customers, or at least weighting the results to account for who is more or less likely to have responded

title: Data entry systemdesign batch job scheduling
topic: Data entry systemdesign batch job scheduling
question: How would you design the scheduling for this set of batch jobs so they run reliably and in the right order?
idealAnswer:
Jobs need explicit dependency ordering, e.g. Job C should only start after Job B succeeds, not just run on a fixed time offset, since a delayed upstream job could otherwise cause Job C to read stale data

A scheduler or orchestrator, e.g. a DAG-based tool, is preferable to independent cron jobs because it can express and enforce these dependencies directly

Each job should have retry logic for transient failures, e.g. a temporary network issue, rather than the whole nightly run failing outright

If a job fails after retries, downstream jobs should not run on incomplete or missing data, the pipeline should stop or alert rather than silently produce a wrong report

Mentions monitoring or alerting so someone is notified when a job fails, rather than the team discovering a problem only when the report looks wrong the next day

title: Data mid domain idempotency pipelines
topic: Data mid domain idempotency pipelines
question: What does it mean for a data pipeline to be idempotent, and why does that matter?
idealAnswer:
An idempotent pipeline produces the same end result no matter how many times it's run with the same input, running it twice shouldn't duplicate or corrupt data

Pipelines fail and get retried or manually rerun often, e.g. after a transient error, so non-idempotent jobs risk inserting duplicate rows or double-counting metrics on rerun

A common technique is to overwrite or upsert a specific partition, e.g. delete-then-insert for a given date, rather than blindly appending new rows

Another technique is deduplication keyed on a natural or synthetic unique identifier, so reprocessing the same record doesn't create a second copy

A strong answer notes idempotency is especially important for backfills and manual reruns, where an operator might not remember exactly what already ran successfully

title: Data mid domain star schema dimensional modeling
topic: Data mid domain star schema dimensional modeling
question: What is a star schema, and why is dimensional modeling still commonly used for analytics even though it's a less normalized design than a typical transactional database?
idealAnswer:
A star schema has a central fact table, e.g. sales transactions, holding measures and foreign keys, surrounded by dimension tables, e.g. product, customer, date, that hold descriptive attributes

It's called a star schema because the fact table sits in the middle with dimension tables radiating outward, joined directly to it

Dimensional models favor query simplicity and performance for analytics, fewer joins, intuitive structure for business users, over the strict normalization used to avoid update anomalies in transactional systems

Denormalizing dimensions, e.g. repeating a product's category name on every row instead of normalizing it further, trades some storage and update overhead for much simpler and faster analytical queries

Contrasts with a snowflake schema, where dimensions are further normalized into sub-dimensions, trading some query simplicity for reduced redundancy

title: Data mid domain streaming vs batch
topic: Data mid domain streaming vs batch
question: What's the difference between batch and stream processing, and what tradeoffs come with choosing streaming?
idealAnswer:
Batch processing operates on a bounded chunk of data collected over a period, e.g. hourly or daily, and processes it all at once

Stream processing operates on unbounded data continuously, as events arrive, producing results with much lower latency

Streaming reduces latency from data generation to insight, which matters for use cases like fraud detection or live dashboards, but is generally more complex to build, operate, and debug than batch

Streaming systems have to handle out-of-order and late-arriving events, e.g. using watermarks and windowing, which batch systems don't need to worry about since all data is already collected

A strong answer notes that many systems use both, e.g. a streaming layer for near-real-time approximate results plus a batch layer that periodically recomputes exact results, sometimes called a lambda-style architecture

title: Data mid domain warehouse vs lake
topic: Data mid domain warehouse vs lake
question: What's the difference between a data warehouse and a data lake, and what is a 'data lakehouse' trying to solve?
idealAnswer:
A data warehouse stores structured, schema-on-write data optimized for fast SQL analytics, typically after transformation

A data lake stores raw data in its native format, structured, semi-structured, or unstructured, at low cost, with schema applied at read time

Warehouses give strong query performance and governance but are expensive and inflexible for very large or unstructured data, e.g. logs, images, JSON blobs

Lakes are cheap and flexible but historically lacked strong transactional guarantees, schema enforcement, and query performance, and could easily become a disorganized 'data swamp'

A lakehouse, e.g. using table formats like Delta Lake or Iceberg, adds warehouse-like features, ACID transactions, schema enforcement, indexing, on top of cheap lake storage, aiming to get the benefits of both

title: Data mid scenario ab test pitfalls sample ratio mismatch
topic: Data mid scenario ab test pitfalls sample ratio mismatch
question: What's going on here, and what should you check before trusting the result at all?
idealAnswer:
This is a sample ratio mismatch, SRM, the observed split, 48,000 vs 52,000, deviates from the intended 50/50 split by more than random chance would explain

An SRM is a red flag that something is broken in the experiment setup, e.g. a bug in the randomization, one variant loading faster and being tracked more, or a bot filtering discrepancy between groups, not something to just ignore

When an SRM is present, the test's results should not be trusted, whatever effect you're seeing is possibly explained by whatever is causing the mismatch rather than the actual product change

Diagnose the SRM before drawing conclusions, e.g. check assignment logs, check if certain user segments were more likely to be excluded or dropped from one arm, check for logging or bucketing bugs

A strong answer knows there's a formal way to test for SRM, e.g. a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test on the observed vs expected split, rather than eyeballing whether the numbers look close enough

title: Data mid scenario late arriving data
topic: Data mid scenario late arriving data
question: How would you redesign this pipeline to handle late-arriving events correctly?
idealAnswer:
Recognize this as a late-arriving data problem: event time, when it happened, differs from processing time, when the pipeline saw it, and the pipeline is currently keying off processing time implicitly

One approach is to allow a grace period, e.g. wait an extra day or two before treating a day's numbers as final, accepting some latency in exchange for more complete numbers

Another approach is to support reprocessing or recomputation, e.g. re-run the aggregation for a given day whenever new late data arrives for it, so numbers are corrected rather than staying wrong

Communicate clearly to stakeholders which numbers are provisional versus finalized, e.g. labeling recent days as 'still updating', so people don't misinterpret a partial number as complete

A strong answer weighs the tradeoff explicitly: waiting longer improves accuracy but delays availability, and mentions that the right grace period should be based on the actual observed distribution of how late data arrives

title: Data mid scenario pipeline failure investigation
topic: Data mid scenario pipeline failure investigation
question: How would you go about diagnosing and fixing this failure, and what would you put in place to reduce the blast radius next time?
idealAnswer:
First check the job logs and error output to identify where and why it failed, e.g. an upstream schema change, a timeout, a resource limit, rather than guessing

Assess the half-written table specifically, since partial writes can be worse than a clean failure, someone querying it now might see incomplete or duplicated data without knowing

A strong answer notes this is exactly why writes should be atomic, e.g. write to a staging table or new partition and swap it in only on success, rather than writing directly into the table readers use

Decide whether to roll back the partial write, mark the table as stale/unavailable, or otherwise prevent it from being read as if it were complete, before fixing the root cause

After identifying the root cause, fix it and consider whether a backfill is needed for the missed run, plus check whether other downstream dependents were affected

For prevention, mentions things like alerting earlier, adding retries for transient failures, making writes atomic/idempotent, and possibly circuit-breaking downstream jobs so they don't run on known-bad upstream data

title: Data mid systemdesign cdc data sync

question: How would you design a system to keep the warehouse in near-real-time sync with the production database, without hammering it with repeated full queries?
idealAnswer:
Recognize that full extraction doesn't scale as data grows, and doesn't meet the near-real-time freshness requirement, a fundamentally different approach is needed, not just running the dump more often

Change data capture, CDC, e.g. reading the database's write-ahead log or replication stream, lets you capture only inserts/updates/deletes as they happen, rather than re-reading the whole table

CDC events get streamed, e.g. through a message queue or streaming platform, and applied incrementally to the warehouse tables, so the warehouse stays close to real-time without repeated full scans

Consider the impact on the source database, e.g. reading from a replica or the replication log rather than issuing large queries against production, to avoid degrading application performance

Handle schema changes on the source gracefully, e.g. a new column added to the production table, since CDC pipelines need to adapt without breaking

title: Data senior domain cap theorem data systems
topic: Data senior domain cap theorem data systems
question: Explain the CAP theorem and how it concretely shapes design decisions in distributed data systems.
idealAnswer:
CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can only guarantee two of three properties during a network partition: consistency, every read returns the most recent write, availability, every request gets a response, and partition tolerance, the system keeps working despite network splits

Since network partitions are a fact of life in distributed systems, partition tolerance is effectively mandatory, so the real tradeoff in practice is between consistency and availability during a partition

A CP system, e.g. many traditional distributed databases with strong consistency, will refuse or delay requests during a partition rather than risk returning stale or conflicting data

An AP system, e.g. many NoSQL stores like Cassandra or DynamoDB in their default modes, will keep serving requests during a partition but may return stale or eventually-consistent data

A strong answer notes CAP is about behavior specifically during a partition, outside of a partition, most systems can offer both, and also that the theorem is a simplification, real systems offer a spectrum, e.g. tunable consistency, not a binary choice

Ties this to a concrete design decision, e.g. choosing an AP system for a high-traffic analytics event pipeline where losing a bit of consistency briefly is fine, versus a CP system for something like financial ledger data where stale reads are unacceptable

title: Data senior domain data lineage governance

question: What is data lineage, and why does it become critical as an organization's data platform grows?
idealAnswer:
Data lineage tracks where a piece of data came from and every transformation it went through, from original source to final table or report, both column-level and table-level lineage are useful

As the number of pipelines and tables grows, it becomes hard for any one person to know how a given metric was actually computed, lineage makes that traceable instead of tribal knowledge

Lineage supports impact analysis, e.g. before changing or deprecating a source table, you can see every downstream table and dashboard that depends on it and would break

Lineage supports debugging, e.g. if a number looks wrong, you can trace backward through the transformation chain to find where the error was introduced

Lineage is also central to governance and compliance, e.g. tracing where personally identifiable information flows through the system, to ensure it's properly access-controlled or deleted on request

title: Data senior domain exactly once vs at least once
topic: Data senior domain exactly once vs at least once
question: What's the difference between at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once processing semantics, and how do real systems actually achieve something close to exactly-once?
idealAnswer:
At-least-once guarantees every message is processed, but a message may be processed more than once, e.g. after a retry following a crash before an acknowledgment was sent

At-most-once guarantees a message is never processed more than once, but some messages may be lost, e.g. if the consumer crashes after receiving but before processing

Exactly-once means every message is processed once and only once, which is genuinely hard to guarantee end-to-end across distributed components, especially when external side effects are involved

In practice, true exactly-once delivery is rarely achieved at the network/transport level, instead systems achieve exactly-once effects by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing, e.g. deduplicating by a unique message ID, or transactional writes, e.g. atomically committing both the output and the offset/checkpoint together

A strong answer gives a concrete mechanism, e.g. Kafka's transactional producer/consumer APIs, or a sink that upserts on a unique key so reprocessing the same message has no additional effect

Notes the tradeoff: exactly-once semantics add complexity and often reduce throughput, so many systems deliberately choose at-least-once plus idempotent consumers as a simpler, more practical path to the same end result

question: How would you plan and execute this backfill safely, given the scale involved and the fact that the system needs to stay operational the whole time?
idealAnswer:
Recompute into a new location, e.g. a shadow table or new partition set, rather than modifying the live table in place, so readers are never exposed to a partially backfilled or inconsistent state

Break the backfill into manageable chunks, e.g. by date range, both to parallelize the work and to allow validation and rollback at a granular level rather than an all-or-nothing operation

Validate the recomputed data against the old data and against independent sources before cutting over, e.g. spot-checking aggregate totals, row counts, and known edge cases, to build confidence the fix is actually correct and didn't introduce new bugs

Plan the cutover itself carefully, e.g. an atomic swap of table/view pointers once validation passes, so consumers see a clean transition at a known point in time rather than data changing under them mid-query

Consider cost and resource impact of reprocessing petabytes of data, e.g. scheduling it to avoid contending with production workloads, and estimate cost/time upfront since this is a large, expensive operation

title: Data senior scenario cost performance tradeoffs data lake
topic: Data senior scenario cost performance tradeoffs data lake
question: The data lake's storage and compute costs have tripled in a year while data volume only doubled. How would you investigate and bring costs back under control without breaking anyone's workflows?
idealAnswer:
Investigate query patterns first, e.g. are queries doing full table scans because of poor partitioning or missing indexes/file-level statistics, small file problems, or lack of predicate pushdown, since compute cost scales with data scanned, not just data stored

Improve file layout and partitioning, e.g. partitioning by commonly filtered columns like date, compacting many small files into fewer larger ones, using columnar formats with good compression, e.g. Parquet, to reduce the volume scanned per query

Address the duplicate ad hoc extracts directly, teams working around slowness by copying data themselves multiplies both storage and inconsistency risk, the underlying slowness needs fixing rather than tolerating the workaround

Consider a caching or materialized aggregate layer for frequently queried patterns, so expensive raw scans aren't repeated for the same common questions

Set up cost attribution and visibility, e.g. per-team or per-query cost tracking, so cost growth isn't invisible until the bill arrives, and teams can be accountable for expensive query patterns

A strong answer balances this against not simply restricting access in a way that blocks legitimate analysis, the goal is efficient access, not less access

Communicate the change and a deprecation timeline to consumers, including a way for unknown or undiscovered consumers to surface themselves, e.g. an announcement plus monitoring for continued reads of the old column

question: How would you design the data pipeline that computes and serves features for this at the scale and latency required?
idealAnswer:
Split the pipeline into an offline/batch path for computing historical features used in training, and an online/streaming path for computing and serving up-to-the-minute features at low latency, since batch computation over history is far too slow for a tens-of-milliseconds serving requirement

Use a streaming layer, e.g. consuming a transaction event stream, to maintain rolling aggregates like 'transaction count in the last hour' incrementally, updating a fast key-value store rather than recomputing from scratch on every request

Ensure the same feature computation logic is shared or kept consistent between the offline training path and the online serving path, otherwise training/serving skew, subtle mismatches between how a feature was computed during training versus at prediction time, silently degrades model quality

Address point-in-time correctness for training data, when generating historical training examples, the features must reflect only what was known at that historical moment, not the current, fully up-to-date value, otherwise the model trains on leaked future information

Design the online store for very low read latency and high throughput, e.g. a low-latency key-value store like Redis, since the model's prediction path is on the critical path of a live transaction

A strong answer addresses failure modes, e.g. what the serving path does if a feature computation is delayed or unavailable, since a fraud model still needs to make some decision even with a stale or missing feature, rather than the transaction path failing entirely

title: Frontend entry domain css box model
topic: Frontend entry domain css box model
question: What is the CSS box model, and how does the box-sizing property change how width and height are calculated?
idealAnswer:
Every element is a box made of four layers, from inside out: content, padding, border, and margin

By default (content-box), width and height apply only to the content area, so padding and border are added on top, making the rendered box larger than the specified width

box-sizing: border-box changes width and height to include padding and border, so the specified size is the final rendered size, which is usually easier to reason about in layouts

Margin is always outside the box and is not included in either box-sizing mode, and adjacent vertical margins can collapse into a single margin

Many teams set a global border-box reset (e.g. on the universal selector) specifically to avoid the surprise of padding/border expanding an element beyond its intended width

title: Frontend entry domain dom event flow
topic: Frontend entry domain dom event flow
question: When you click on a nested element, how does the browser decide which event handlers run, and in what order?
idealAnswer:
The DOM is a tree, and a click dispatches an event that travels through three phases: capturing (root down to target), target, and bubbling (target back up to root)

By default, addEventListener attaches handlers to the bubbling phase, so a handler on a parent fires after the handler on the clicked child

Passing { capture: true } attaches the handler to the capturing phase instead, so it runs on the way down, before the target's own handler

event.stopPropagation() stops the event from continuing to bubble (or capture) further, while event.preventDefault() stops the browser's default action but does not stop propagation, these are separate concerns

Event delegation exploits bubbling: attaching one listener to a common ancestor and checking event.target lets you handle events for many, or dynamically added, children without binding a listener to each one

title: Frontend entry domain http caching cors
topic: Frontend entry domain http caching cors
question: From a frontend developer's point of view, what do HTTP caching headers and CORS each control, and why do they matter when building a web app that talks to an API?
idealAnswer:
Caching headers like Cache-Control (e.g. max-age, no-cache, no-store) tell the browser and intermediate caches how long a response can be reused before it must be re-fetched or revalidated

ETag and Last-Modified support revalidation, letting the browser ask 'has this changed?' and get a cheap 304 Not Modified instead of re-downloading the full response

Poorly set caching can cause stale UI (users seeing old data or old JS bundles after a deploy) or wasted bandwidth (nothing being cached at all)

CORS is a browser-enforced security mechanism controlling whether JavaScript running on one origin can read a response from a different origin, the server opts in via Access-Control-Allow-Origin and related headers

CORS errors happen client-side in the browser console even though the request often actually reached the server, the fix is on the server (or a proxy), not something the frontend can bypass alone

Preflight OPTIONS requests are sent automatically by the browser for 'non-simple' requests (custom headers, certain methods/content-types) to check permissions before the real request is sent

title: Frontend entry domain semantic html a11y
topic: Frontend entry domain semantic html a11y
question: Why does it matter whether you use semantic HTML elements (like <button>, <nav>, <header>) instead of generic <div>s styled to look the same?
idealAnswer:
Semantic elements carry built-in meaning that assistive technology (screen readers) uses to announce roles, landmarks, and navigation structure, a div styled as a button has no inherent role announced to a screen reader

Semantic elements come with free, correct default behavior, a <button> is keyboard-focusable and activates on Enter/Space by default, a div requires manually adding tabindex, role, and key handlers to match

Using the right element reduces the amount of ARIA needed, ARIA should supplement, not replace, native semantics, and incorrect ARIA can make accessibility worse than none at all

Semantic structure (headings, landmarks like <nav>/<main>/<footer>) lets screen reader users jump directly to the section they want instead of linearly reading the whole page

Semantic HTML also benefits SEO and browser features like reader mode, it is not solely an accessibility-only concern, it is a general correctness practice

title: Frontend entry domain state vs props
topic: Frontend entry domain state vs props
question: In a component-based UI framework like React, what's the difference between state and props, and how does changing each one affect what re-renders?
idealAnswer:
Props are data passed down from a parent component to a child, they are read-only from the child's perspective, the child cannot modify its own props directly

State is data owned and managed internally by a component, it can change over time in response to user interaction or other events, and the component controls its own state

Changing a component's state triggers that component (and typically its children) to re-render, changing a prop passed into a component also triggers a re-render of that component

Data generally flows one way, down through props, so when a child needs to affect a parent, the parent passes a callback function down as a prop for the child to call

Lifting state up, moving state to the closest common ancestor of components that need to share it, is the standard pattern when two sibling components need to stay in sync

Open the browser's performance profiler to confirm where time is actually being spent, rather than guessing, it might be layout/paint, JS execution, or something else entirely

Check whether every keystroke triggers a full re-render of all 2,000 items rather than only re-rendering what changed, and whether list items are missing stable keys, causing unnecessary re-creation

Consider debouncing or throttling the filter input so filtering logic runs after typing pauses, rather than on every single keystroke

Consider list virtualization (rendering only the rows currently visible in the viewport) since rendering thousands of DOM nodes at once is expensive regardless of framework

Check if expensive work (like the filter/search logic itself) is being recomputed from scratch each render instead of memoized, and whether it could run in smaller chunks or off the main thread

idealAnswer:
Each component should expose a small, clear set of props (e.g. variant, size, disabled) rather than letting callers pass arbitrary styles, to keep usage consistent

Shared design tokens (colors, spacing, typography) should live in one place and be consumed by all components, instead of hardcoded values duplicated per component

Components should be composable, e.g. a Button should work standalone or inside a Form, without hidden dependencies on where it's rendered

Include sensible accessible defaults (focus states, keyboard handling, ARIA attributes) baked into the components themselves so every consumer gets them for free

Plan a versioning or update story from the start, so changing a shared Button doesn't silently break every page that uses it

question: How would you design basic client-side routing for a small single-page app with a handful of pages, like Home, Profile, and Settings?
idealAnswer:
Map URL paths to components so the browser's URL bar reflects the current view, using the History API (pushState/replaceState) rather than only changing state in memory

Support browser back/forward buttons correctly by listening for popstate, so navigation feels native rather than breaking the browser's expected behavior

Handle direct loads and refreshes of non-root URLs (e.g. /settings) correctly, this usually requires server or static-host configuration to serve the app shell for any path, not just the router changing on the client

Consider code-splitting each route so the JS for Settings isn't downloaded until the user actually navigates there, keeping the initial load light

Think through what happens for routes that don't match anything (a 404/not-found view) and routes that require auth (redirecting unauthenticated users)

Preserve scroll position appropriately, e.g. resetting scroll on navigation to a new page but restoring it when the user goes back

title: Frontend mid domain event loop async
topic: Frontend mid domain event loop async
question: Explain how the JavaScript event loop handles asynchronous work, and specifically the difference between microtasks and macrotasks.
idealAnswer:
JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack, the event loop coordinates running code, handling events, and executing queued asynchronous callbacks without blocking that thread

Macrotasks (also called tasks) include things like setTimeout callbacks, DOM events, and I/O, each macrotask runs to completion before the loop moves on

Microtasks include promise callbacks (.then/.catch/.finally) and queueMicrotask, the microtask queue is fully drained after each macrotask finishes and before the next macrotask or render, even before the next setTimeout(fn, 0)

This is why Promise.resolve().then(...) logs before a setTimeout(fn, 0), even though both are 'async', microtasks always get priority over the next macrotask

Because the loop is single-threaded, a long-running synchronous task blocks everything, including rendering and other callbacks, which is why expensive synchronous work causes a frozen/unresponsive UI

async/await is syntactic sugar over promises, an async function still runs synchronously up to the first await, and code after await is scheduled as a microtask continuation

title: Frontend mid domain memoization rerenders
topic: Frontend mid domain memoization rerenders
question: In a framework like React, what actually causes a component to re-render, and how do memoization tools help, and how can they backfire?
idealAnswer:
A component re-renders when its own state changes, when its parent re-renders (by default, children re-render too, regardless of whether their props changed), or when context it consumes changes

React.memo (or equivalent) skips re-rendering a component if its props are shallow-equal to the previous render, this only helps if the parent would otherwise re-render it unnecessarily

useMemo caches an expensive computed value between renders, and useCallback caches a function reference, both exist mainly to keep referential equality stable so memoized children (or dependency arrays) don't invalidate unnecessarily

Overusing memoization has real costs: added code complexity, memory to store cached values, and the comparison itself has a cost, memoizing a cheap computation can be net slower than just recomputing it

A common mistake is memoizing a component but still passing it a new inline object, array, or function as a prop each render, which breaks the shallow-equality check and defeats the memoization entirely

Profiling (e.g. React DevTools Profiler) should drive where memoization is applied, rather than applying it reflexively everywhere

title: Frontend mid domain rendering pipeline
topic: Frontend mid domain rendering pipeline
question: Walk through what happens in the browser's rendering pipeline between a CSS/JS change and pixels updating on screen, and why some changes are more expensive than others.
idealAnswer:
The pipeline generally goes style (recalculate which CSS rules apply), layout/reflow (compute geometry, position and size of every element), paint (fill in pixels), and composite (combine painted layers on the GPU)

Changing layout-affecting properties (width, position, font-size) forces layout to be recomputed, which cascades to paint and composite, this is the most expensive path

Changing paint-only properties (background-color, visibility) skips layout but still requires a repaint of the affected area

Changing composite-only properties (transform, opacity) can skip both layout and paint if the element is already promoted to its own layer, this is why animating transform/opacity is much cheaper than animating top/left or width

Reading layout properties (like offsetHeight) right after writing styles forces a synchronous layout recalculation ('layout thrashing'), doing this repeatedly in a loop is a classic performance bug

Browsers batch DOM changes and only actually run this pipeline once per frame, ideally hitting 60fps (about 16.7ms per frame) for smooth animation

title: Frontend mid domain state management tradeoffs
topic: Frontend mid domain state management tradeoffs
question: When would you keep state local to a component versus lifting it into some form of global/shared state management? What are the real tradeoffs?
idealAnswer:
Local state is simpler, more encapsulated, and easier to reason about, it should be the default for state that only one component (and maybe its direct children) cares about, like an input's current value or a dropdown's open/closed state

Global state becomes worth the added complexity when multiple, distant parts of the tree need to read or update the same data, and prop-drilling it through many intermediate components becomes painful

Global state introduces costs: harder to trace where an update came from, larger re-render surface if not carefully scoped, more boilerplate, and a steeper learning curve for new contributors

Server-derived data (API responses) is often a different category than UI state, tools built for caching/syncing server state (like React Query) handle staleness, refetching, and caching concerns that generic global state stores don't solve well

Context alone is fine for rarely-changing, broadly-needed values (like theme or auth user), but using Context for frequently-changing state can cause broad, hard-to-control re-renders unless combined with proper memoization or a dedicated state library

The decision should be driven by actual sharing needs and update frequency, not by defaulting to global state for everything upfront

title: Frontend mid scenario accessibility audit
topic: Frontend mid scenario accessibility audit
question: You've been asked to run an accessibility audit on an existing product page before launch. What would you actually check, beyond running an automated tool?
idealAnswer:
Automated tools (like axe or Lighthouse) only catch a fraction of real issues, roughly the mechanically checkable ones like missing alt text or contrast ratios, they can't judge whether alt text is actually meaningful or whether a flow makes sense

Test full keyboard navigation manually: can every interactive element be reached and operated with Tab/Shift+Tab/Enter/Space/Arrow keys alone, is focus order logical, and is the currently focused element always visibly indicated

Test with an actual screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA, or similar) on the key user flows, not just individual elements, to check that headings, landmarks, form labels, and dynamic content announcements make sense as a coherent experience

Check that dynamic UI updates (toasts, validation errors, loading states) are announced to assistive tech, e.g. via aria-live regions, not just visually shown

Check color contrast in context (including on hover/focus/disabled states, not just default state) and confirm no information is conveyed by color alone

Check that modals and dropdowns trap focus appropriately while open and restore focus to a sensible place when closed

title: Frontend mid scenario fetch race condition
topic: Frontend mid scenario fetch race condition
question: What's going wrong here, and how would you fix it?
idealAnswer:
This is a classic race condition, requests fired in order can resolve out of order over the network, so the last response to arrive wins even if it's not for the latest query

One fix is to track a request identifier (or the query itself) at fetch time, and when a response comes back, only apply it if it still matches the current/latest request, discarding stale ones

Another fix is to use an AbortController to actually cancel the in-flight previous request when a new one starts, avoiding wasted work and any risk of the stale response being applied

Debouncing the input so a request is only fired after the user pauses typing reduces how often this race can occur, but doesn't fully eliminate it since network timing is still not guaranteed

Mentions that many data-fetching libraries (like React Query or SWR) handle request deduplication and cancellation for exactly this class of problem, which is a good argument for not hand-rolling fetch logic for something like this in a larger app

title: Frontend mid scenario memory leak debug
topic: Frontend mid scenario memory leak debug
question: Users report the tab gets slower and slower the longer they leave your app open, and eventually the browser tab crashes. How would you track this down?
idealAnswer:
Use the browser's memory profiler to take heap snapshots at different points in time and compare them (e.g. after navigating between views repeatedly) to see which object types keep growing

Look for classic leak sources: event listeners added on mount but never removed on unmount, timers/intervals not cleared, and subscriptions (WebSocket, observers) not torn down when a component unmounts

Check for detached DOM nodes, elements removed from the visible tree but still referenced by a closure or a global variable, which prevents garbage collection

Check for growing caches or arrays that accumulate data across navigations without ever being cleared, e.g. an in-memory log or cache with no eviction policy

Reproduce deliberately by navigating between the same two views many times and watching whether memory climbs monotonically, versus climbing and settling, which narrows down whether it's a true leak or just normal variance

title: Frontend mid scenario third party script slowdown
topic: Frontend mid scenario third party script slowdown
question: How would you diagnose this, and what options would you consider to fix it without just removing the feature?
idealAnswer:
Confirm the cause first using the performance panel or a tool like WebPageTest/Lighthouse, checking whether the third-party script is blocking the main thread, delaying other resources, or shifting layout after load

Check how and when the script is loaded, a synchronous <script> tag in the head blocks parsing, switching to async or defer (or loading it after the page's own critical content) reduces its impact on initial render

Consider lazy-loading non-critical widgets (like a chat bubble) until after the main content is interactive, or until a user interaction signals intent (e.g. scroll, hover)

Consider using a web worker or a facade/placeholder pattern (showing a lightweight static stand-in that loads the real, heavy widget only on interaction) to defer the actual cost

Check for layout shift caused by the widget injecting itself into the page after load, reserving space for it upfront prevents CLS regressions

Communicate the measured tradeoff back to the stakeholders who requested the script, performance budgets should be a shared, visible constraint, not something engineering absorbs silently

title: Frontend mid systemdesign client caching strategy
topic: Frontend mid systemdesign client caching strategy
question: Design a client-side caching strategy for an app where several screens display overlapping data fetched from the same API, e.g. a user's profile shown in a header, a sidebar, and a settings page.
idealAnswer:
Introduce a shared client-side cache keyed by resource identity (e.g. by user id) so multiple components requesting the same data reuse one cached entry instead of firing duplicate requests

Define a staleness policy per resource type, some data (like a user's display name) can be cached longer than something like a live notification count, this shouldn't be one-size-fits-all

Handle cache invalidation explicitly: when a mutation updates the user (e.g. editing settings), the cache entry must be updated or invalidated so all screens reflect the change, not just the screen that made the edit

Deduplicate in-flight requests, if two components request the same uncached resource simultaneously, they should share one network request rather than firing two

Decide a fallback/loading strategy: show stale-while-revalidate (old data immediately, refreshed in background) versus a loading spinner, this is a real UX tradeoff, not just an implementation detail

Mentions that this is largely a solved problem via libraries like React Query, SWR, or Apollo's cache, and a strong answer explains why to use one of these vs. hand-rolling it, or explicitly justifies hand-rolling for a specific reason

title: Frontend mid systemdesign design system architecture
topic: Frontend mid systemdesign design system architecture
question: Design the architecture for a design system that will be shared across three separate product teams, each with their own codebase and release cadence.
idealAnswer:
Publish the design system as a versioned, independently installable package (e.g. via npm) rather than shared source files copied between repos, so each team controls when it upgrades

Separate design tokens (colors, spacing, typography as data) from components, so tokens can be themed or reused even by teams not consuming the full component library

Define a clear API contract per component (props, slots, events) and treat breaking changes with semantic versioning and a deprecation path, since three teams on different cadences can't all update in lockstep

Build in accessibility and cross-browser behavior once, centrally, so consuming teams inherit it for free instead of re-solving it

Provide strong documentation and live examples (Storybook or similar), plus visual regression testing, so the system's own maintainers can catch unintended visual changes before publishing

Establish a governance process for how consuming teams request new components or changes, balancing system consistency against individual team velocity, this is often the harder problem than the technical implementation

title: Frontend mid systemdesign infinite scroll feed
topic: Frontend mid systemdesign infinite scroll feed
question: Design the client-side architecture for an infinite-scroll social feed, similar to a typical timeline, that stays smooth even after the user has scrolled through thousands of posts.
idealAnswer:
Use an IntersectionObserver (or scroll-position calculation) on a sentinel element near the bottom to trigger fetching the next page, rather than listening to every scroll event, which is expensive and imprecise

Use cursor-based pagination (based on an opaque cursor or timestamp/id) rather than offset-based pagination, offsets shift and cause duplicate or skipped items if new posts are inserted while scrolling

Virtualize the rendered list (rendering only DOM nodes for posts near the viewport) so memory and rendering cost stay flat instead of growing unbounded as thousands of posts accumulate

Handle images and media lazily, loading media only as items approach the viewport, to avoid huge upfront bandwidth and memory use

Decide how to handle new content arriving at the top while the user is scrolled deep into the feed, typically buffering it behind a 'new posts' affordance rather than silently shifting content underneath the user

Plan for error and retry states per page fetch, and preserve scroll position correctly if the user navigates away and back

title: Frontend senior domain bundle splitting strategy
topic: Frontend senior domain bundle splitting strategy
question: At scale, how would you think about bundle size and code-splitting for a large web app with dozens of routes and many contributing teams?
idealAnswer:
Route-based code splitting is the baseline, each route's JS should load only when that route is visited, rather than shipping the entire app's code on first load

Beyond routes, split further on genuinely rarely-used or heavy code, like a rich text editor, a charting library, or a modal only some users trigger, loaded lazily on demand rather than in the main bundle

Watch for shared-dependency duplication across split chunks, if multiple lazy chunks each bundle their own copy of a large library, splitting can backfire, proper vendor/shared-chunk configuration avoids this

Set and enforce a performance/bundle-size budget in CI so a single PR can't silently regress load time, catching bloat before it ships rather than after users complain

Use real bundle analysis tools (like a bundle analyzer/treemap) to find and address unexpectedly large dependencies, rather than guessing, a single misused import can pull in a much larger library than intended

Consider that code-splitting has a UX cost too, waterfall requests for the split chunks introduce latency, and needs to be balanced against prefetching strategies (e.g. prefetching likely-next routes on hover or idle time)
